items.t: Nokia's Satellite Pact With ICEYE Eyes Ukraine as AI Networking Orders Surge
sum: Nokia shares closed Wednesday at €7.00, up 3.5%, as the Finnish telecom equipment maker pressed ahead on several fronts — a freshly signed satellite communications memorandum with Ukraine, deepening AI networking ties, and a quarterly report that showed robust profit growth alongside a more cautious cash-flow outlook.

The Helsinki-based company and satellite operator ICEYE signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's defense ministry on October 22. Under the arrangement, the two firms will explore possible cooperation on sovereign satellite communications for the country. Nokia was careful to frame the document as a scoping exercise rather than a contract already awarded for building out a satellite network.

The satellite news landed a day after Nokia flagged progress in its work with NVIDIA on artificial intelligence. The company unveiled a sovereign platform built around agent-based AI for running telecom networks autonomously, and separately reported advances toward commercial deployment of AI in radio access networks. Field trials in live networks and customer programs are said to be edging toward operational use.

On the customer side, Hotwire Communications selected Nokia on Wednesday to construct a next-generation network in North Carolina, designed to be ready for AI-driven network architectures. Hotwire expects the network to go live in early 2027, putting the project's timeline into next year.

The broader market backdrop was friendlier for AI-linked names on Wednesday, with shares tied to artificial intelligence recovering from a broad selloff. AP reported gains among companies connected to the construction of AI data centers. That coverage describes the sector environment only — the agency did not cast Nokia as a driver of the move, nor did it explicitly attribute the stock's advance to the recovery among those firms.

In its quarterly report roughly two weeks ago, Nokia posted third-quarter 2026 revenue of EUR 5,154 million, a 10% increase year over year. Comparable operating profit climbed 35% to EUR 605 million. The customer business in AI and cloud was the standout: revenue there jumped 123%, with order intake up 118%.

sum: Nokia said on Wednesday, November 4, 2026, that artificial intelligence could drive almost half of global network traffic by 2035. The forecast comes from the company's new Global Network Traffic Report, published in Espoo and carried by GlobeNewswire.

Nokia projects total network traffic will nearly quadruple from 2026 levels to almost 3,789 exabytes per month in 2035. AI is expected to account for 44 percent of that traffic, changing the requirements for networks that have traditionally been built mainly around downloads.

The report distinguishes between traditional application traffic and newer workloads generated by autonomous agents, connected machines and physical AI. Nokia expects physical AI applications, including robots and vehicles, to generate more than 90 percent of their network traffic through uplinks by 2035.

Agentic AI traffic is projected to reach 160 times its 2026 level by 2035, while physical AI traffic is expected to reach 105 times its 2026 level. For network operators and equipment suppliers, the projections point to a more varied demand profile, ranging from large data uploads to continuous, real-time connections.

Nokia also expects data processing to become more distributed. Edge and metro-core infrastructure could handle 36 percent of all AI-native traffic by 2035, as lower latency, more efficient models and data-sovereignty requirements push intelligence closer to users and connected devices.

The report supports Nokia's strategic focus on connectivity infrastructure for AI applications, but it is a company forecast rather than a financial commitment or customer order. Its investment relevance therefore depends on whether operators convert expected traffic growth into spending on radio, fixed, IP, optical, core and data-center networks.

Nokia Chief Technology and AI Officer Pallavi Mahajan said networks would need to support machines that place new demands on uplinks and require real-time responses. She said network readiness should be central to AI planning, while Nokia is building distributed infrastructure intended to support the next phase of AI deployment.

Nokia Corp (NYSE: NOK) shares extended their rally on Thursday, rising 2.81% to $10.63, as investors continued to re-evaluate the company’s valuation based on its expanding role in artificial intelligence infrastructure. The surge followed the release of second-quarter results that exceeded consensus estimates, with management raising the full-year profit outlook. This shift in sentiment highlights Nokia’s transition beyond its traditional telecommunications identity to become a key beneficiary of the AI boom.

The company reported net sales of 4.82 billion euros ($5.60 billion) for the quarter, representing an 8% year-over-year growth. Adjusted earnings per share came in at eight cents, surpassing the expected seven cents. Network Infrastructure revenue grew by 12%, fueled by significant gains in Optical Networks (+19%) and IP Networks (+15%). These operational improvements underpin the raised guidance provided by CEO Justin Hotard.

A critical driver of this performance was the explosive growth in AI and Cloud revenue, which doubled (+103%) to account for 9.3% of total sales. This segment was supported by 2.8 billion euros in new AI and cloud orders. Hotard highlighted this expansion as evidence of Nokia’s increasing reach into high-growth infrastructure markets, distinct from its legacy telecom business.

Addressing potential headwinds, Hotard outlined a strategy to mitigate memory shortages expected through 2027. The plan involves securing long-term supply deals, adjusting product designs, and passing higher costs to buyers. These measures aim to protect margins amid constrained component availability.
The divergence between the overall revenue growth (8%) and the AI/Cloud segment growth (+103%) indicates a structural shift in Nokia’s revenue mix.

sum: Nokia's latest quarterly report landed with a thud: the shares shed 14% yesterday. But the sell-off says less about whether the Finnish equipment maker is winning AI business than about what it costs to deliver it. Orders are piling up. Cash is not keeping pace. That gap, more than any verdict on demand, is what investors are now being asked to price.

Revenue from AI and cloud customers jumped 123% year on year in the third quarter of 2026 at constant currency. Orders from that same client group reached EUR 1.5 billion, up 118%. These are not vague aspirations about a future market — they are booked sales and signed contracts.

The growth is anchored in specific network hardware. IP Networks expanded 43% at constant currency, while Optical Networks added 18%. Taken together, Nokia expects those two segments to grow 25–30% in 2027.

Comparable operating profit rose 35% to EUR 605 million, lifting the corresponding margin to 11.7%. Read in isolation, that looks like a quarter that should have been rewarded rather than punished. The market, though, is not grading the three months just ended. It is trying to work out what it will cost to fill the next round of orders.

Reported operating profit came in at just EUR 196 million. Restructuring and other charges of EUR 357 million account for much of the distance between that figure and the EUR 605 million adjusted number. Adjusted earnings are a useful lens on the underlying business — but they should not become a parallel universe in which recurring overhaul costs stop counting. A strategically sensible restructuring still consumes real money.

That distinction matters because Nokia has trimmed its forecast for how much of comparable operating profit will convert into free cash flow in 2026, cutting the range to 35–55% from 55–75%. The demand side is not the immediate problem. The question is how much of the profit actually reaches the bank.

Two separate burdens explain the shortfall, and investors should not conflate them. Nokia plans EUR 400 million in additional working capital to keep supply flowing for further growth. On top of that, it now expects restructuring costs of roughly EUR 1.1 billion, up from an earlier EUR 800 million. One ties up money in day-to-day operations; the other weighs on the company's overhaul.

sum: Nokia Oyj (NOK) shares surged as much as 6% in Thursday trading after the Finnish telecom equipment maker said it was deepening its collaboration with Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) to build what the companies call an agentic, unified data foundation for automating telecom networks.

The expanded partnership combines Nokia Data Suite, a packaged set of telecom data products with built-in quality controls and semantic modeling, with Microsoft Fabric, the software giant's unified analytics platform. The goal, according to Nokia, is to let carriers pull trusted network data in minutes rather than the weeks it can currently take, dramatically speeding up the preparation of network information for AI applications.

Investors responded quickly. Nokia shares climbed to $10.715 in early trading with turnover of roughly $206 million, extending a rally that has lifted the stock nearly 70% so far in 2026. The broader market was also supportive, with S&P 500 futures up 0.8%.

The solution is designed for multi-vendor, cross-domain telecom environments and supports public cloud, hybrid cloud, and on-premises deployments. That flexibility allows operators to advance automation while complying with different regulatory frameworks across markets. Nokia said the integrated platform is already commercially available, with additional autonomous-network deployments planned as the partnership matures.

Early deployments will concentrate on three operational scenarios. The first is autonomous Voice over New Radio, or VoNR, assurance, where AI agents detect service problems, analyze root causes, and recommend corrective actions. The second is geo-experience analysis, which uses AI to pinpoint users suffering poor wireless performance and identify coverage or capacity hotspots across radio access networks, covering both network-slice customers and regular 4G and 5G subscribers.

The third area is predictive maintenance and fault management, where agents blend historical and real-time data to flag potential failures before they affect customers. Nokia also described an AI operations assistant that functions as a copilot for network engineers, providing contextual insights, suggested actions, and automated workflow execution.

Much of the bull case hinges on Nokia’s ability to convert AI network deals into durable free cash flow. The collaboration with Nvidia on AI Radio Access Network technology represents one of the most tangible proof points. AI RAN aims to embed machine learning directly into the radio access layer of mobile networks, potentially reducing energy consumption and improving spectral efficiency. If the technology gains commercial traction, it could support the kind of multi-year cash flow trajectory the DCF model bakes in.

Execution risk, however, remains a live concern. Large-scale infrastructure and defense projects carry notoriously lumpy revenue profiles and margin pressure, factors that may limit how much value investors are willing to assign today.

sum: The strategic picture at Nokia is becoming clearer by the week: this is a company methodically rebuilding itself around the infrastructure demands of the artificial-intelligence boom. The latest piece of that puzzle came into place with a binding agreement to acquire NXP Semiconductors' Chandler fabrication plant in Arizona — a move designed to secure in-house production of indium-phosphide optical chips, a component class that is growing increasingly critical as AI data centers expand. The transaction is structured in two stages: Nokia will initially lease capacity at the facility from the start of 2027, with the full takeover slated for the first quarter of 2029. The logic is straightforward — controlling its own supply chain for a strategically vital component rather than relying on external vendors.

That announcement landed on the same day Nokia unveiled its first commercial AI-RAN platform, developed in partnership with Nvidia and Dell and aimed at future 6G networks. The Finnish network equipment maker also joined forces with Qatar's Ooredoo on the Zankore AI platform for the Asia-Pacific region, an initiative spearheaded by Indonesian operator Indosat alongside Nvidia. The project targets the construction of one gigawatt of capacity for a so-called Nvidia DSX AI Factory. Taken together, these moves sketch out a company that is positioning itself across multiple layers of the AI infrastructure stack — from the chips inside the hardware to the radio access networks that carry the traffic.

For all the strategic momentum, the market response has been notably muted. In Frankfurt, Nokia shares were trading at €8.07, down 2.11 percent on the day, while the Helsinki listing also drifted lower against a largely flat broader index. sum: Nokia Corporation NOK has secured a multi-year contract with Orange Belgium to upgrade the latter's transport network, strengthening its position in advanced telecom infrastructure and optical networking. The deal expands Nokia's role in supporting high-capacity connectivity as demand rises from AI, cloud computing, 5G, streaming, gaming and remote work.

Under the agreement, Nokia will serve as the sole supplier for Orange Belgium's large-scale network modernization project. The company will combine the operator's fixed and mobile transport systems into a converged optical network, improving efficiency, resiliency and service readiness for future high-bandwidth services.

Nokia will deploy its 1830 Photonic Service Switch platform (PSS), supporting speeds from 1G to 400G and beyond for faster and more reliable data transmission across Belgium. It will also provide its AI-powered WaveSuite automation software to simplify network management, improve operational performance and speed up service delivery.
With global telecom operators accelerating next-generation infrastructure investments, Nokia is likely to capitalize on growing modernization opportunities, supporting its long-term growth prospects.

The AI and Cloud book-to-bill was noted to be approximately 3 times during the Q1 earnings call Q&A, translating to €3 of orders that Nokia collected for every €1 that the company booked for revenue in that segment.
